findings.description: The diff correctly centralizes ConfigError handling so a hand-edited bad config.toml reads as exit 2 ("cannot evaluate") instead of exit 3 ("crash") on every verb, not just the three that already special-cased it — a real and narrowly-scoped fix, and it does not collide with the three verbs that already catch-and-return-2 themselves (they never rethrow, so the outer branch never double-handles them). But the change is left half-finished: `main`'s own docstring still states unconditionally that "an exception escaping a verb is printed with its backtrace ... and returns 3", which the new branch now falsifies for the whole ConfigError class, and nothing in test/ pins the new exit-2-no-backtrace path. For a package whose entire discipline is that a docstring is the contract and every behaviour change gets a test, shipping the behaviour change without touching either is exactly the kind of gap this instrument exists to catch.
findings.after: `err isa Config.ConfigError && (println(stderr, "gbg ", key, ": ", sprint(showerror, err)); return 2)` is now checked FIRST: a ConfigError escaping any of the ~21 verbs that do not catch it themselves is printed WITHOUT a backtrace and returns 2, not 3 — exactly contradicting the docstring's own "an exception escaping a verb ... returns 3" one paragraph above the new code.
findings.before: "An exception escaping a verb is printed with its backtrace to `stderr` and returns 3, so a crash is never read as a finding" (main()'s docstring, unchanged by this diff) — and every verb's ConfigError, if not caught locally, hit only the generic branch below and returned 3.
findings.why_it_matters: A concrete input that was previously valid to trigger: run any verb other than `config`, `doctor` or a `design *` verb (e.g. `gbg round bank`, `gbg preflight ...`) against a hand-edited `.gbg/config.toml` with a bad key. Before this diff that verb crashed with a backtrace and exit 3; after it, the same input now exits 2 with a one-line message and no backtrace. That is the right fix (the PR's own comment says so, and it is real: only cmd_config, a Doctor check and Design.design_verb caught ConfigError themselves before), but `main`'s docstring — the one place a reader learns the CLI's own exit-code contract — was left asserting the old, now-false blanket claim, and no test in test/ (grepped for ConfigError/backtrace/"crashed —" near Main) exercises the new branch to pin the exit code or the message shape.
findings.title: main()'s own docstring is now false for a ConfigError, and no test covers the new branch
findings.evidence: Docstring (src/CLI/Main.jl, unchanged): "An exception escaping a verb is printed with its backtrace to `stderr` and returns 3, so a crash is never read as a finding". findings.description: The underlying fix is right: a structurally bad consumer config is exit 2 by D8, and most verbs reported it as a crash. But the edit is wider than that defect. Placed in main()'s catch-all it cannot distinguish a ConfigError thrown before the verb did anything from one thrown after the verb rewrote the consumer's config, and it deletes the backtrace for both. The two post-write re-reads (Bump.jl:36, Init.jl:565) are exactly the case where exit 3 carried information nothing else carries. No test was added: the testset that owns main()'s exit contract is itself in this change set and enumerates the other exit codes case by case, so the new branch is the one arm of that contract with no oracle.

findings.why_it_matters: The stated defect is narrow: `Config.read` at a verb's ENTRY throws on a hand-edited config, and only three verbs (cmd_config, cmd_doctor, design_verb) mapped that to the documented exit 2. The edit fixes it at the outermost frame instead, so it also swallows a ConfigError raised anywhere else in a verb's body. Two such sites are in the tree today: `gbg bump` writes the new pin into .gbg/config.toml and THEN calls `Config.read(root)` (Bump.jl:36), and `gbg new` calls `Config.read(root; check = false)` on the config `init` just rendered (Init.jl:565). If the tool renders a config it cannot read back — a template defect, a bad substitution, a path the renderer got wrong — the operator now sees `gbg bump: config error: …` and exit 2, "cannot evaluate", the same line a hand-edited config produces, with the half-rewritten config.toml left on disk and the backtrace (the only thing naming Bump.jl:36 as the frame) discarded. Exit 3 existed to say "this is the tool's fault, here is where"; that signal is now unavailable for the whole ConfigError class, and CLAUDE.md makes exit codes the contract a log is never grepped to replace. Narrowing the catch to the config-read boundary — or to verbs that have written nothing yet — would fix the stated defect without covering the post-write reads.
findings.title: The ConfigError→exit 2 arm sits at main()'s outermost catch, so a config the TOOL just wrote is reported as the user's bad config, without a backtrace

findings.description: The defect the comment names is that ConfigError from the initial config read escaped as exit 3 in every verb but three. A defect-sized fix catches it where the config is read (or wraps the read), leaving genuine mid-verb ConfigErrors as crashes with their backtrace. The edit instead catches the class for the whole verb table, so it changes the exit code and suppresses the backtrace for failures that are NOT "the user handed me a bad config" — specifically the ones where the tool wrote the config itself moments earlier. Both the behaviour (3 → 2) and the diagnostics (backtrace → one line) change for input that was valid before. The fix's own comment claims only the read case ("reported a hand-edited config.toml as exit 3"), so the widening is undeclared.

findings.why_it_matters: The intended case is right and is a real fix: `gbg round bank <round>` against a hand-edited .gbg/config.toml returned 3 ("crash") before and returns 2 ("cannot evaluate") now, which is what the CLI's own contract at Main.jl:109 and :122 promises. But the arm keys on the exception CLASS, not on the config-read call site, so it also catches a ConfigError thrown deep inside a verb that has already changed the tree. The concrete previously-working input: `gbg bump 1.0.1` rewrites the `[tool] version` line of .gbg/config.toml (Bump.jl:35) and immediately re-reads it (Bump.jl:36); when that re-read throws — a config the tool itself just produced and cannot validate — the run previously printed `crashed —` with a backtrace and exit 3, the correct signal that this is a tool defect with a half-applied bump on disk. It now prints a single `config error:` line and exit 2, the same output a user gets for standing in a non-consumer directory, and the backtrace that would localise the defect is suppressed. The same shape applies to any future verb that writes the config and re-reads it. Exit codes are this package's contract and a log is never grepped for a verdict, so an operator or a skill gate cannot tell "your config is bad" from "the tool corrupted your config" any more.

findings.description: One of the two exemptions removed was implicated in the BLOCKER (`in`), the other was not (`of`), and the commit removes both. The test's own comment concedes the second: "Neither operator is ever followed by a template literal in these scripts" and "no such form occurs in the eleven scripts or the prelude (checked 2026-09-12)" — i.e. the `of` exemption protected nothing and, symmetrically, its removal catches nothing that exists. This is a guard made wider than the defect required, on a frozen-script surface where every future edit must pass it. Note a side effect neither the comment nor the new assertions mention: because the lookbehinds match the last three characters and not a word, `(?<!in )` and `(?<!of )` had also been exempting every word ENDING in "in " or "of " ("within", "again", "proof"), so the tightening is broader than the two keywords named.

Removing `(?<!of )` as well takes a JavaScript form with it: `for (const x of `abc`)` — a non-interpolated template literal iterated directly — was accepted by this guard before and now turns `Pkg.test()` red, as does a bare backtick after "of" inside an ordinary single-quoted JS string (`description: 'one of `a` or `b`'`), which is valid JavaScript that closes nothing. The exposure is small and the authors measured it ("no such form occurs in the eleven scripts or the prelude"), and I confirmed it: running the head regex over all eleven scripts plus instruments/prelude.js with comments stripped as the test strips them yields zero matches. Filed as a nit because the widening is real but currently costs nothing, and the workaround (escape the backtick) exists.

The docstring is the reader-visible statement of the contract, and it was left saying the old thing while the code now does the new thing.

findings.evidence: Base main() docstring (git show af1adec6c6666be0c687ffd32bbc9145fecef580:src/CLI/Main.jl): "An exception escaping a verb is printed with its backtrace to `stderr` and returns 3, so a crash is never read as a finding" — unchanged at head, while the code added: "err isa Config.ConfigError && (println(stderr, "gbg ", key, ": ", sprint(showerror, err)); return 2)" before the unconditional `return 3` path.

findings.description: The fix-pass commit c7db4e5 presents itself as a complete, categorised inventory of what it fixed (RATIONALE/SRC/SCRIPTS/REGISTERS, 8+7+6+4=25 items covering 28 of 37 findings), but its actual diff touches two files — templates/README.md and docs/src/guide/install.md — that appear in none of the four paragraphs. Both edits are individually sound (verified against the current templates/SKILL.md.tmpl file and the install.md @ref target), so this is not a behaviour or contract defect; it is a gap between what the commit claims to account for and what it actually changed, the specific shape this lane is built to surface.
findings.after: templates/README.md: "Two exceptions: `queue-guard.sh.tmpl`...; and `SKILL.md.tmpl` carries the ordinary Markdown header but NOT on the first line — it follows the mandatory YAML frontmatter..." / install.md gains: "A **consumer** is a package that pins this tool and is reviewed by it — one of the four GBG science packages, or the tool itself, which is its own fifth consumer."
findings.before: templates/README.md: "One exception: `queue-guard.sh.tmpl` is copied byte-for-byte from PF's Stop hook and carries no header, so the upstream text stays comparable; the sidecar hash is what marks it managed." / docs/src/guide/install.md had no consumer gloss at all.
findings.why_it_matters: The commit's own message partitions its 25 named edits into exactly four buckets (RATIONALE 8, SRC 7, SCRIPTS 6, REGISTERS 4) and states the pass closed 28 of 37 banked findings "by class, not by line" — a precise, auditable accounting. Neither of these two real, substantive file edits is named anywhere in that accounting; templates/README.md is not mentioned in this commit's message or any later one in the range, and install.md's gloss surfaces only two commits later (36788aa), described in the past tense as something "I glossed... at its first use in install.md" without ever being credited in c7db4e5 itself. In an instrument whose entire design point is that self-certifying commit messages are claims and not evidence, a commit that enumerates its own scope and then silently exceeds it by two files is exactly the failure mode this lane exists to catch — even though both edits are, on their merits, legitimate and narrow.
findings.title: c7db4e5's own itemized claim omits two of its own files
findings.evidence: c7db4e5 diffstat lists `templates/README.md | 8 ++++---` and `docs/src/guide/install.md | 2 ++` among its 18 changed files, but grepping the full commit message body for "template", "README", "install.md" or "consumer" finds no match; the only later trace is 36788aa's message: "pages#2: I glossed \"consumer\" at its first use in install.md and left the bare uses..." — crediting the fix to a different commit's retrospective, not to c7db4e5 itself.

locations: src/CLI/Doctor.jl:253, src/CLI/Preflight.jl:848, src/CLI/Rounds.jl:69 (the rendered pass/refusal strings)
findings.description: The base text used one word, "pinned or managed", for a set that genuinely holds two kinds, and splitting it was warranted. But the split as written misclassifies its own pivot: the sidecar the MANAGED kind is read from is listed under the PINNED kind whose defining property is that the tool never renders it. `Doctor.pinned_and_managed` builds exactly this list — the four `.gbg/` files, the hats, the sub-env manifests, then `Sync.read_sidecar` keys — so the code draws no such line and the distinction exists only in the prose that now claims to explain it. Either `managed.json` belongs to the MANAGED kind, or the PINNED kind needs a definition that admits a file the tool writes but never re-renders from a template.
findings.after: `git status --porcelain` shows none of them modified, in two kinds the one word does not separate — a PINNED file the consumer owns and the tool never renders (`.gbg/config.toml`, `exemptions.toml`, `hats/*.toml`, `seeds.toml`, `managed.json`, every sub-environment `Project.toml` listing the tool) and a MANAGED file `gbg sync` renders and hash-checks thereafter (the SKILL stubs, the rendered policy)
findings.before: `git status --porcelain` shows none of the pinned or managed files modified — `.gbg/config.toml`, `exemptions.toml`, `hats/*.toml`, `seeds.toml`, `managed.json`, every sub-environment `Project.toml` listing the tool, the SKILL stubs, the rendered policy
findings.why_it_matters: `.gbg/managed.json` is the sync sidecar: `Sync.sync` "rewrites `.gbg/managed.json`; idempotent" (src/CLI/Sync.jl:607) and the record writer adds an entry per managed file (Sync.jl:652). Placing it on the side defined as "the consumer owns and the tool never renders" — and, in the docstring, "the consumer writes it once" — teaches the opposite of what the tool does with the one file that defines the other kind. The same two-kind wording is now the text a user sees when `CFG.TORN` passes and when `preflight` and every `gbg round` verb refuse, so the misfiling is the CLI's own explanation of why it stopped, and a consumer reading it would conclude a sidecar modified in the working tree could not have come from `gbg sync`.
findings.title: The new PINNED/MANAGED taxonomy files the sync sidecar `.gbg/managed.json` under "the tool never renders", which `gbg sync` rewrites on every run
findings.evidence: src/CLI/Doctor.jl:231-234 (new docstring) — "A PINNED file the tool never renders: the consumer writes it once and the tool must never see it drift outside its own write path — `.gbg/config.toml`, `.gbg/exemptions.toml`, `.gbg/seeds.toml`, the sync sidecar itself, …" against src/CLI/Sync.jl:607 — "rewrites `.gbg/managed.json`; idempotent" and Sync.jl:652 `files[file * "#gbg:managed"] = Dict("template" => …, "sha256" => sha256hex(block))`.

findings.description: The addition is defensible bookkeeping — ARCHITECTURE §12.B has always listed RULE.CIT.NO_INACCESSIBLE as SCAN.DEAD_REF's second rule, and the scan's own header names both — and `panel` is retained, so the debt is not erased. What drifts is the strength of the promise: a rule whose check was a declared reading-panel debt now reads as program-checked, on one surface of many and through a scan the ledger indexes under a different rule. The same shape applies to the sibling edit at RULE.DOC.API_GROUPING (SCAN.API_PAGE_STRUCTURE's canonical rule is RULE.DOC.INTERNAL_API), though there the surfaces do match the rule's scope.
findings.why_it_matters: `check` is defined as what catches the rule's next violation, and the rule binds "on any user-facing surface". SCAN.DEAD_REF is registered with `surfaces = ["src"]` and its body filters to `surface_kind(cfg, f) == :julia`, so an inaccessible citation on a rationale page, a guide page or a README is not covered by the scan now standing in front of the panel. Worse for a consumer: `Scan.apply_ledger` resolves a `scope = "policy"` exemption against the scan's CANONICAL rule only (`rule = row["rule"]`, here RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS), so waiving RULE.CIT.NO_INACCESSIBLE leaves the named scan running under another rule's name, while waiving RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS silently removes the check this rule now claims to have.
findings.title: RULE.CIT.NO_INACCESSIBLE's check now names a src-only scan whose canonical rule is a different one, so a policy waiver of either rule misses
findings.evidence: catalog/scans.toml:302-306 — `id = "SCAN.DEAD_REF"` / `rule = "RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS"` / `surfaces = ["src"]`; src/Scan.jl:351-353 — `id = row["id"]; rule = row["rule"]` then `for e in Ledger.entries(ledger, rule; scope = "policy")`; policy/RULES.toml:449 statement — "Never cite an inaccessible source … on any user-facing surface."

findings.description: Two of the three header changes are real corrections — `quote_probe` and `class_candidates` are sent (Passes.jl:544) and `rulebook_summary` is sent nowhere, so removing it was right. The third pair goes the other way: the one key present in every act-verifier args file was dropped from the list, and an optional key the CLI never writes was added to it. This is the smallest kind of contract drift, but it is drift introduced by an edit whose stated point was to make the header match the args.
findings.why_it_matters: These headers are the only written contract between `Passes.pass_open`, which builds the args, and the frozen script that consumes them; the audit-changes and bug-hunt scripts even cite their schema file beside the list. After the edit the header understates what arrives (`round_dir` is in `base` and survives into `act`; only the bug-hunt architecture verifier deletes it) and overstates what may arrive (`batch` appears nowhere in src/ — `const BATCH = Math.max(1, A.batch || 6)` is served only by its own default). A maintainer trimming the CLI to the documented list would remove a key that is sent, or wire a `batch` knob the CLI has no place to set.
findings.title: verify-act.js's rewritten args header drops `round_dir`, which the CLI always sends, and adds `batch?`, which no CLI path ever sends
findings.evidence: src/CLI/Passes.jl:543 — `base = Dict{String,Any}("schema_version" => 1, "round" => round, "round_dir" => dir, "pass_dir" => pd, …)`; :581 — `act = merge(base, Dict("range" => fixrange, …))`; the only removal is :609 `delete!(a, "adjudicated_titles"); delete!(a, "strength"); delete!(a, "round_dir")`, in the bug-hunt branch. `grep -rn batch src/` returns nothing; verify-act.js:109 `const BATCH = Math.max(1, A.batch || 6)`.

locations: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:2484 (§12.B SCAN.ID_RESOLVES row, edited in the same diff)
findings.description: This is the lens's classic direction — an exact quantifier weakened to a vague one — with a real justification attached, so I report it at nit rather than pressing it as a defect. The concern is the inconsistency within one edit: if a measured figure goes stale the moment it is written, the ID_RESOLVES figures are as stale as the signature figures were; if a dated snapshot is acceptable, the signature figures could have been dated too. One of the two treatments should be the house convention.
findings.after: this package takes `names`, the form all but a handful of its docstrings already used … Narrowed to `names` on 2026-09-12, the form this package's docstrings had almost entirely taken already; `SCAN.SIGNATURE_TYPED` re-measures it, so no count is carried here
findings.before: 451 arguments over 247 docstrings here take `names` and 4 took `mirror` (2026-09-12) … Narrowed to `names` 2026-09-12, the form 247 of 251 docstrings here already took
findings.why_it_matters: Dropping a cited count is what RULE.TEST.COUNTS_REMEASURED asks for ("A count nothing asserts is re-measured, never cited"), and SCAN.SIGNATURE_TYPED does exist and does re-measure (catalog/scans.toml:142, src/Scans/signature_typed.jl:49). But the same diff kept the other cited-count site in the same document — SCAN.ID_RESOLVES' "964 references, 11 unresolved … 17 of the 24 cases … 143 of 1705" — and merely dated it. A reader of §12 now meets two conventions for the same class of claim with no rule stated between them, and the evidence for the 2026-09-12 narrowing (how many docstrings it actually had to change: four) survives only in the exemption ledger and the work queue, not in the design record that records the decision.
findings.title: The signature-types measurement was replaced by "a handful" while the ID_RESOLVES counts beside it were kept as a dated snapshot
findings.evidence: policy/RULES.toml:533 — `statement = "A count nothing asserts is re-measured, never cited; a drop is a finding."`; the surviving §12.B text at docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:2484 — "Measured over this package on 2026-09-12, before it was built: 964 references, 11 unresolved … Those figures are that day's snapshot; the scan re-measures on every run".

Grepping the whole corpus for '@ref install' confirms only three of the five guide pages carrying the word 'consumer' actually link it.
